headline: Standardize: The Best Way We Know Today
alternativeHeadline: The first chapter of Part Seven, opening Standardize, the fifth of the six S's. Four S's have made the home sorted, arranged, clean, and safe, but almost all of it lives in one person's head and hands; this chapter delivers the concept of a standard, the best way you know today written down, a recipe and not a rule, and reads the friction meter as a HOLD with a new catch behind the needle, the first thing that keeps a gain from sliding back.
description: Chapter 23 is the first chapter of Part Seven and opens Standardize, the fifth of the six S's. Four S's have made the home sorted, arranged, clean, and safe, and yet almost all of that lives in exactly one place: you. You know the best way to load the dishwasher, the order of the bedtime routine, the trick that keeps mornings calm, and none of it was written down, so the home works beautifully right up until the day you are sick, away, or out of patience, and then it quietly stops. That is the gap the fifth S closes. Things drift back not because anyone is careless but because a way that lives in one head is invisible to everyone else, so everyone does it their own way and the best way stays a secret; the people who first named these steps, on the factory floors of Toyota, gave this S the blunt job of preventing reversion back to the old way, not through willpower or nagging but by making the good way visible and shared. A standard is how you make the best way visible. The chapter's hero is that a standard is a recipe, not bureaucracy: the best way you know to make something turn out right, written down so it turns out right every time, for anyone, even on a tired day. Like a recipe it is a gift, taking skill that lived in one person's hands and making it available to anyone who can read. The definition, frozen: a standard is the current best way to do a recurring task, written down plainly enough that anyone in the home can follow it and get the same result, and kept open enough that it is rewritten the moment a better way is found. A standard is measured by use, not thoroughness, usually a few plain lines about one task, and the test is whether the next person actually follows it and gets the result you would have gotten. The word doing the quiet work is today: a standard is not the last word, it is the current best word, and the moment someone finds a better way, the standard is not broken, it is simply what you improve, so it is a starting point, not a finish line, and the thing that makes improvement stick rather than a cage. The living-standard line, frozen: a standard is not a rule carved in stone, it is the best way you have found so far, held in place only until you find a better one, and then rewritten without ceremony. To write your first standard, pick a small recurring task that mostly works only when you do it, watch yourself do it once and write the steps in plain words, as few as will do the job (most home tasks are three to six steps; step eleven means you are describing personal quirks), and put it where the task happens, not in a folder, so the next person meets it at the moment they need it; the shortcut is to ask the person who already does it best to teach it, because the best way usually already exists, fully formed, in somebody's hands. Because writing down the best way changes nothing in the rooms, the friction meter holds exactly where Safety left it and does not move; but for the first time something appears behind the needle, a catch, a ratchet, holding it against the pull back toward friction. Every gain until now was quietly reversible, a sorted room re-clutters, a clean surface re-soils, a habit lapses; a written standard is the first thing that blocks the backslide. The needle did not advance today; it got something arguably more valuable, it stopped being able to retreat. This is a hold with a new anti-backslide catch, not a move and not a milestone, and the goal stays ahead on the calm side, because Standardize has only begun and Sustain still follows. The rule, frozen: a standard is the best way you know today, written down. Chapter 24, Checklists, Schedules, and Responsibilities, continues Part Seven by turning standards into their tools.
